m-serratus-posterior-inferior.summary: A thin serrated muscle beneath latissimus dorsi running to the lower ribs.
facts: Spinous processes of T11–L2 (via the thoracolumbar fascia)
Lower borders of ribs 9–12
Intercostal nerves 9–11 and subcostal nerve
Posterior intercostal arteries, subcostal artery
Pulls the lower ribs down and back

m-iliocostalis.summary: The lateral column of the erector spinae, with lumbar, thoracic and cervical parts.
facts: Iliac crest, back of the sacrum, lumbar spinous processes (common tendon) and angles of the lower ribs
Angles of the ribs and transverse processes of C4–C6
Posterior rami of the spinal nerves
Dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal and lumbar arteries
Both sides: extend the spine; one side: bends it to the same side
tus: The erector spinae columns from lateral to medial: iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis ('I Love Spine').

m-longissimus.summary: The longest and thickest, middle column of the erector spinae, running from the sacrum to the skull.
facts: Common tendon (sacrum, lumbar spinous processes), thoracic and lower cervical transverse processes
Thoracic and cervical transverse processes, lower ribs and mastoid process (longissimus capitis)
Posterior rami of the spinal nerves
Posterior intercostal and lumbar arteries; in the neck the occipital and deep cervical arteries
Extends the spine and head; acting on one side it bends to the same side, and longissimus capitis turns the head to the same side

m-spinalis.summary: The most medial and thinnest column of the erector spinae; it links the spinous processes together.
facts: Spinous processes of the upper lumbar and lower thoracic vertebrae
Spinous processes of the upper thoracic and cervical vertebrae (spinalis capitis: occipital bone)
Posterior rami of the spinal nerves
Posterior intercostal arteries
Extends the spine

m-splenius.summary: A muscle with head (capitis) and neck (colli) parts that wraps the deep back muscles like a bandage.
facts: Lower half of the nuchal ligament, spinous processes of C7–T6
Splenius capitis: mastoid process and lateral 1/3 of the superior nuchal line; splenius colli: transverse processes of C1–C3
Posterior rami of the middle cervical spinal nerves
Occipital artery, transverse cervical artery
Both sides: extend the head and neck; one side: turns and tilts the head to the same side
tus: SCM turns the head to the opposite side, splenius capitis to the same side; the two act as synergists in rotation.

m-semispinalis.summary: The most superficial layer of the transversospinal group, spanning 4–6 segments; its head part is the strongest extensor of the back of the neck.
facts: Transverse processes of C7–T12 (semispinalis capitis: C4–T6)
Spinous processes of higher cervical and thoracic vertebrae; semispinalis capitis: occipital bone (between superior and inferior nuchal lines)
Posterior rami of the spinal nerves
Posterior intercostal, occipital and deep cervical arteries
Extends the head and spine; acting on one side it rotates to the opposite side
tus: The greater occipital nerve pierces semispinalis capitis to reach the skin of the back of the head.

m-multifidus.summary: The middle layer of the transversospinal group, made of bundles spanning 2–4 segments; it is thickest in the lumbar region.
facts: Sacrum, PSIS, lumbar mammillary processes, thoracic transverse processes, articular processes of C4–C7
Spinous processes of vertebrae 2–4 segments higher
Posterior rami of the spinal nerves
Posterior intercostal and lumbar arteries
Stabilises the spine segment by segment; extension and rotation to the opposite side
clinical: Lumbar multifidus atrophies in chronic low back pain; it is the target muscle of stabilisation exercises.

m-rotatores.summary: The deepest layer of the transversospinal group: short muscles running from a transverse process to the lamina of the vertebra one or two levels above.
facts: Transverse processes of the vertebrae
Lamina and root of the spinous process of the vertebra 1–2 segments above
Posterior rami of the spinal nerves
Posterior intercostal arteries
Rotation and stabilisation of the spine; proprioception of spinal position
tus: They are best developed in the thoracic region; because of their dense muscle spindles they act mainly as sensory (proprioceptive) organs.

mm-levatores-costarum.summary: Small triangular muscles descending from the thoracic transverse processes to the rib below; they have short and long bundles.
facts: Transverse processes of C7–T11
Between the tubercle and angle of the rib one below (short) or two below (long)
Posterior rami of spinal nerves C8–T11
Posterior intercostal arteries
Raise the ribs (assist inspiration); lateral flexion and rotation of the spine

m-rectus-capitis-posterior-major.summary: A muscle running from the spine of the axis to the skull; it forms the superomedial border of the suboccipital triangle.
facts: Spinous process of the axis
Lateral part of the inferior nuchal line
Suboccipital nerve (posterior ramus of C1)
Vertebral artery, occipital artery
Extends the head and rotates it to the same side

m-rectus-capitis-posterior-minor.summary: A small muscle from the posterior tubercle of the atlas to the occipital bone; it has a connective tissue bridge to the dura mater.
facts: Posterior tubercle of the atlas
Medial part of the inferior nuchal line
Suboccipital nerve (posterior ramus of C1)
Vertebral artery, occipital artery
Extends the head
tus: The role of the myodural bridge between it and the dura mater in cervicogenic headache is debated.

m-obliquus-capitis-superior.summary: A muscle from the transverse process of the atlas to the occipital bone; it forms the superolateral border of the suboccipital triangle.
facts: Transverse process of the atlas
Occipital bone between the superior and inferior nuchal lines (lateral part)
Suboccipital nerve (posterior ramus of C1)
Vertebral artery, occipital artery
Extends the head and bends it to the same side

m-obliquus-capitis-inferior.summary: A muscle from the spine of the axis to the transverse process of the atlas; despite its name it is the only suboccipital muscle that does not attach to the skull.
facts: Spinous process of the axis
Transverse process of the atlas
Suboccipital nerve (posterior ramus of C1)
Vertebral artery, occipital artery
Rotates the atlas (and head) to the same side (atlanto-axial rotation)
tus: The suboccipital triangle is bounded by rectus capitis posterior major and obliquus capitis superior and inferior; it contains the vertebral artery and suboccipital nerve. The greater occipital nerve emerges below the lower border of this muscle.

m-subclavius.summary: A small cylindrical muscle beneath the clavicle running to the 1st rib; it protects the vessels and nerves beneath it.
facts: Junction of the 1st rib and its cartilage
Middle 1/3 of the inferior surface of the clavicle (subclavian groove)
Nerve to subclavius (C5–C6)
Thoraco-acromial artery (clavicular branch), suprascapular artery
Steadies the clavicle and draws it down and medially
tus: In a clavicle fracture it protects the subclavian artery and vein and the brachial plexus beneath it from sharp bone fragments.

mm-intercostales-externi.summary: The most superficial muscle layer of the intercostal spaces; their fibres run downwards and forwards (like hands in pockets).
facts: Lower border of the rib above
Upper border of the rib below; in front, between the costal cartilages, they continue as the external intercostal membrane
Intercostal nerves (T1–T11)
Posterior and anterior intercostal arteries
Raise the ribs (inspiration)

mm-intercostales-interni.summary: The middle layer beneath the external intercostals, with fibres running downwards and backwards (at right angles to the external ones).
facts: Lower border of the rib above (outside the costal groove)
Upper border of the rib below; behind, they continue as the internal intercostal membrane
Intercostal nerves (T1–T11)
Posterior and anterior intercostal arteries, internal thoracic artery
Lower the ribs in forced expiration; the interchondral part assists inspiration
